A.explanation: $P = Fv$ is true for a constant force parallel to velocity, but it is derived from the definition and is not the general definition.

B.explanation: Work done per unit time is already power, so multiplying it again by force does not give power and has incorrect units.

C.explanation: Force per unit time multiplied by velocity has units of $\text{N s}^{-1}$ times $\text{m s}^{-1}$, which is not watts ($\text{J s}^{-1}$).

D.explanation: This states $P = W/t$, the rate of transfer of energy by doing work, which is the definition of power.

hints: Notice the question asks for the definition of power, so look for work done or energy transferred per unit time with unit watt ($\text{J s}^{-1}$).
Recall the governing relation $P = W/t$ and that $P = Fv$ follows from $W = Fx$ only when force is constant and parallel to velocity.
Check the units in the other wordings: multiplying force by work per unit time, or using force per unit time times velocity, does not give $\text{J s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Identify what is needed: the general definition of power, not a special-case formula that is sometimes equal to power.
State the physical rule: power is the rate of doing work or rate of energy transfer, $P = W/t$, measured in $\text{W}$ or $\text{J s}^{-1}$.
Show where $Fv$ comes from: for constant force in the direction of motion, $W = Fx$, so $P = Fx/t = Fv$, which is a useful result but not the definition.
Reject the mixed wordings: option B multiplies force by a quantity that is already power, and option C uses rate of change of force times velocity, so neither means work per unit time.
Only the rate at which work is done matches $P = W/t$ exactly. This is option D
